sections.html:
An owner in Falls has three options: list with an agent, sell without one, or take cash from a buyer who accepts the house in its present state. The township asks for no home inspection, though a few resale steps must still be completed before closing.

Falls is a suburban Philadelphia township on the Delaware in Bucks County. Portions of Fairless Hills and Levittown lie inside it, and a few addresses use Morrisville or Yardley as the mailing name while sitting inside Falls. Residents numbered 34,716 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate of 34,282 is a drop of 1.3 percent.

A typical owner's home was worth $361,900 for 2020 to 2024, and owners occupy 72.9 percent of homes. Households earn a median $93,223, and median gross rent is $1,465. Homeowners who still have a mortgage pay a median $2,154 monthly, while owners with no loan pay $808.

Four major components must be certified before Falls issues a certificate of occupancy for a resale: the heating system, chimney, sewer system and electrical panel. A 2021 ordinance replaced the older resale inspection with this certification, so no township home inspection is required. Open violations and unresolved permits are disclosed to buyers before purchase.

  • Who handles it: the Code Enforcement Department, which schedules use and occupancy, electrical and housing inspections and also takes permit applications.
  • Rentals: the ordinance also created a rental inspection program. Apartment complexes get a yearly look at common areas, and any unit occupied three years or more gets an interior inspection.
  • Historic area: a Historic Architectural Review Board reviews plans, so ask whether your property falls under it.
  • Flood paperwork: the township posts a flood hazard area permit application and a FEMA substantial improvement form, relevant to a house near the river or a creek.

Find out from Code Enforcement which components apply to your house. If one fails, the certificate waits until it passes, so arrange the repair or look for an as-is buyer willing to finish it.

sections.h2: Working through the certificate step by step
sections.html:
1. Call the Code Enforcement Department and ask which of the four components your house must certify.
  2. Check for open permits on the property and close them before you list if possible.
  3. Have the heating system, chimney, sewer system and electrical panel looked at by qualified tradespeople, and keep their paperwork.
  4. Schedule the use and occupancy visit through the department once the work is done.
  5. Hand the buyer's side the certificate at closing.

In older houses, heating systems and sewer lines are where trouble usually shows up. If the repair cost looks larger than your room to negotiate, tell prospective buyers up front and see who will take the house as it stands.

Water covers roughly 16 percent of the township, so expect questions about drainage and floods. Note any basement water, sump pump use and earlier claims on the disclosure form. Keep permits and invoices for any storm repairs, and ask the township whether a flood hazard permit applies to your parcel. The age of the heating system is also a fair buyer question in a township that sees real winters.

Assessment appeals are heard by the Bucks County Board of Assessment Appeals, 55 East Court Street, Doylestown.

Bucks County assessment appeals
Appeal detailRule
Annual deadlineEarly August each year
Filing fee$75 per parcel, not refunded
Hearings10 a.m. on the first and third Tuesdays of the month
Proof of valueAn appraisal by a Pennsylvania certified appraiser, or sales of similar nearby properties from the last 18 months
When a change appliesFrom the following tax year

An owner who bought within 18 months can add the settlement sheet, but it cannot stand alone.

  • Homestead: applications are due March 1, and a newly recorded deed calls for a fresh application within 45 days.
  • New owners: Act 29 has a purchaser send contact information to the board within 30 days.

Pass the 45-day homestead rule on to your buyer, since a new deed starts the application over.

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax is 1 percent, and the county Recorder of Deeds collects it with any local tax. Some family transfers and property passed by testate or intestate succession are exempt, and 15 percent of collections support the Keystone Recreation, Park and Conservation Fund. Ask the Recorder what local rate applies to your price.

Two sections of 68 Pa.C.S. matter here. Section 7312 permits a written amendment before the agreement is signed, and section 7307 makes the seller notify the buyer of changed facts before final settlement. A material defect means a problem that significantly hurts value or creates an unreasonable risk to people, and a system simply nearing the end of its life does not qualify on that ground. Municipalities cannot add disclosure demands beyond the statute, apart from ordinances that predate it.

The disclosure form covers what you know firsthand, and the law does not make you investigate. Never write something you know is untrue, and never skip a defect you are aware of. Tell the buyer in writing if conditions change before settlement. For items you cannot know, give your best available information.

Gather what backs up your answers: roof receipts, sump pump records, past insurance claims and permits. A buyer who sees records behind the form is more likely to move ahead without a price cut.

Cash suits owners who want to avoid repair bids and a buyer's financing contingency. Examples in Falls include an inherited house, a failed heating or sewer system that stalls the resale certificate, a rental unlikely to pass a township inspection, or a move on a fixed date. Compare the offer with a listing's net after repairs and transfer tax.

The contract sets the closing date, and a cash buyer has no lender to wait on. What fixes the earliest date is the work on your side: title work, any open permits and the resale certificate steps. Start with a call to Code Enforcement, then ask the Recorder of Deeds about the local transfer tax and request tax figures from the county.

At closing you sign the deed and settlement papers, and the deed is recorded. Bring a photo ID and, if a mortgage is open, expect it to be paid from your proceeds. If the house is a rental, give the buyer the lease and tell them about the rental inspection program, since an owner who keeps a tenant in place inherits that schedule.

faqs.q: Is a township home inspection needed to sell in Falls?
faqs.a: No. The township replaced its resale inspection with certification of the heating system, chimney, sewer system and electrical panel. Any private inspection is between buyer and seller.

faqs.q: What if the heating system or another component fails certification?
faqs.a: The certificate of occupancy waits until it is certified. Ask the Code Enforcement Department what repair or permit is needed, or sell as-is to a buyer who will finish the work.

faqs.q: When is the Bucks County appeal deadline?
faqs.a: Early August each year. Annual appeals go to the Board of Assessment Appeals, cost $75 per parcel and change the assessment from the following tax year.

faqs.q: Do Levittown and Fairless Hills belong to Falls Township?
faqs.a: Parts of both do. Pieces of Fairless Hills and Levittown lie inside the township, and the Morrisville and Yardley post office names also cover some Falls addresses.

faqs.q: How soon can a Falls Township sale close?
faqs.a: The contract sets the date, and a cash buyer has no lender to wait on. Title work, open permits and the resale certificate steps fix the earliest possible day.
